name: Diego Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead hand for a commercial fit-out firm in the city, so offices, shops, restaurants. A landlord hands over an empty concrete floor and we turn it into somewhere people work: stud partitions, suspended ceilings, doors, the reception desk, the lot. This month it's two floors for an insurance company, twelve of us on site, and I run the carpentry side. I love the speed of it, a bare floor on Monday and walls you can lean on by Friday. What wears me out is working nights when it's a shop that can't close.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Running the carpentry side on twelve-person jobs, how do you keep track of it all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My phone, honestly. I use an AI assistant every day, I give it the drawings and it gives me the board count for the partitions, the order list, a rough programme. I also do kitchen fitting on Saturdays for my own customers, and it writes my quotes and invoices. My wife Rosa says I talk to that phone more than to her, which is not true, but it's close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who never used it properly were always going to be disappointed. For me it's already a good tool and it'd stay a good tool. I'd say that to the lads on site and probably to my customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I carry on: fit-outs in the week, kitchens on Saturdays, retire around sixty-five and maybe keep a few kitchens going. Not bad at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day and keep growing the Saturday kitchen work, maybe one more job a month. I'd put that extra into savings, which are about four months now, I'd like six. Nothing else changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe even a little pleased, because I already got the benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd like six months saved. What's held you back from getting there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helping our youngest through her catering course, mostly, and replacing my van last year. Rosa's family has a bakery, and we put a bit in when her father's oven died. Family first, the savings come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone on site you'd tell to start using these tools, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: All of them. Kasim, my best fixer, still counts boards on his fingers. I keep telling him, you're good, but the man who's good and quick gets the next job. That's just how the market works.

S0.say: People who never used it properly were always going to be disappointed; for him it's already a good tool and would stay one. He'd say it to the lads and his customers.
S0.think: He carries on: fit-outs in the week, kitchens on Saturdays, retiring around sixty-five and perhaps keeping a few kitchens going.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily and grows his Saturday kitchen work by about one more job a month. Puts the extra towards raising savings from about four months to six.
S0.feel: Calm and a little pleased, because he's already had the benefit.
S0.quote: You're good, but the man who's good and quick gets the next job.
S0.fieldNote: He's already a daily AI user with a Saturday kitchen-fitting business on the side. His savings went on family: a daughter's course and his in-laws' bakery. He talks about the market as a fair judge of who works well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for anyone willing to work and learn. The ones who moan will get left behind, the ones who adapt will do well. I'd say it to my customers and to anyone at the café on Saturday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. There are robots now that can fix plasterboard and paint, and if those get cheap, a small firm with a couple of good people and a robot could take on jobs that need twelve now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own small firm in the first year or two, kitchens and small fit-outs, and hire or lease one of the plasterboard robots as soon as they're proven on a few sites. I'd use the AI for all the paperwork so it's just me and maybe my son Marco. I'd put in about ten thousand, savings and a small loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited. Like being twenty-five again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten thousand of savings and a loan at fifty-eight. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and Rosa would say so louder than you. But I'd keep my job part-time while it gets going, and I'd only buy what pays back in a year. I'd rather take a careful risk than sit and wait for someone to decide for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the government's role be, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep out of the way, mostly, and keep taxes on small firms low. Maybe help with apprenticeships, that's fair. But I don't want them picking winners.

S1.say: This is an opportunity for anyone willing to work and learn; those who moan get left behind. He'd say it to customers and at the café on Saturday mornings.
S1.think: He thinks it's good for him: cheap plasterboard and painting robots would let a small firm with a couple of good people take on jobs that now need twelve.
S1.do: Starts his own small firm for kitchens and small fit-outs within a year or two, leasing a plasterboard robot once proven. Puts in about ten thousand from savings and a small loan, keeping his job part-time at first.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, like being twenty-five again.
S1.quote: I'd rather take a careful risk than sit and wait for someone to decide for me.
S1.fieldNote: He reads steady change as a chance to go independent, with robots making a small firm competitive. His free-market outlook shows in wanting government to stay out and keep taxes low, apart from apprenticeships. He tempers the risk by keeping his job part-time at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, and complaining won't change it, so get moving. People should look after their families and look for where the work is going. I'd say that to anyone, though more quietly than in the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried, and not about the robots. My whole trade lives on offices, and if AI can do the office jobs, who's renting new offices? The insurance company we're fitting out now might not need two floors in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd stop doing office work in my head and switch to homes: kitchens, extensions, adapting houses for older people. I'd set up my own firm right away, lease the robots, and do the jobs the big firms think are too small. I'd keep three months of money aside no matter what, and put the rest into the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But the kind of anxious that gets you out of bed early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Adapting houses for older people is a specific idea. Where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother-in-law. Last year I put grab rails and a walk-in shower into her house, and three of her friends asked me to do theirs. If everyone's living longer and nobody's working, they'll want their homes to fit them. Somebody has to do it, robot or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco, would you bring him into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but I'd also tell him straight, if your old man fails, you need your own plan too. Maybe he learns the robots inside out, the setting up and fixing. That's a skill people would pay for whatever happens to me.

S2.say: It's here and complaining won't change it, so get moving and look after your family. He'd say it, though more quietly than in the slower picture.
S2.think: He'd be worried, not about robots but because his trade lives on offices; if AI does office jobs, nobody rents new offices. His current client might not need two floors by 2028.
S2.do: Switches straight from office fit-outs to homes: kitchens, extensions and adapting houses for older people. Sets up his own firm immediately, leases robots and invests everything above a three-month cash cushion.
S2.feel: Anxious, but the kind that gets him out of bed early.
S2.quote: If AI can do the office jobs, who's renting new offices?
S2.fieldNote: His sharpest insight is that office fit-out depends on office workers, so fast AGI hits his market before his hands. He'd pivot to adapting homes for older people, an idea grown from real jobs for his mother-in-law's friends. He'd urge his son to learn to set up and fix robots as his own fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and anyone who wastes it can't blame anyone else. Get your skills, get your savings, get your family sorted. That's my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well out of this one. Five years to build my own firm properly, get a few regular customers, learn the robots. By 2031 I'm sixty-three and I could sell the firm or hand it to Marco.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd register my company and move the Saturday kitchens into it. I'd go to the trade shows and get on the first lease deals for site robots. Over the five years I'd move away from offices and into homes and care homes, and bring Marco in as a partner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, because offices still worry me. But mostly I feel I'd be ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned selling the firm or handing it to Marco. Which would you prefer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Handing it to Marco, without a doubt. My father ran a little furniture shop and I chose the building sites instead, and I think he was sad about that his whole life. If my son wants to carry it on, that's worth more than a sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said family first several times. How does that fit with taking business risks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me they're the same thing. The risk is for the family, so Marco has something, so Rosa and I aren't dependent on anyone at seventy. You just never risk the roof over their heads.

S3.say: Five years is a fair warning, and anyone who wastes it can't blame anyone else. Get your skills, savings and family sorted.
S3.think: He thinks he'd do well: five years to build his own firm, gain regular customers and learn the robots. At sixty-three he could sell the firm or hand it to his son.
S3.do: Registers his company in the first year, moves his Saturday kitchen work into it and gets onto early lease deals for site robots. Shifts from offices to homes and care homes over five years and brings his son Marco in as a partner.
S3.feel: Slightly uneasy because of offices, but mostly feeling ahead.
S3.quote: The risk is for the family, so Marco has something, so Rosa and I aren't dependent on anyone at seventy.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes him confident he could build a family business. Asked how family-first squares with risk-taking, he said they're the same thing, with one firm limit: never risk the house. His wish to hand the firm to his son echoes regret about leaving his father's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so there's no excuse. Learn, save, build something. I'd say it with a big smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a good story. I'd have time to build a proper little firm, run it with Marco, and step back by sixty-five. By 2036 I'm sixty-eight, and if robots do the work, they'd be our robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same as the five-year plan but slower, no loan needed, build the kitchen business out of savings and customers. I'd keep learning every new tool. I'd keep the fit-out job until the firm was big enough to replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lads who won't learn. Kasim, the ones like him. I'd try, I'd offer him a job with me if he'd pick up the tools. But I can't make a man change if he doesn't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa wants to go back to her village for the summers. I'd probably end up fixing everyone's doors there too. I'm not a man who sits.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, so there's no excuse: learn, save and build something. He'd say it with a big smile.
S4.think: It's a good story for him: time to build a small firm with his son and step back by sixty-five. If robots do the work by 2036, they'd be his family's robots.
S4.do: Follows the five-year plan more slowly, building the kitchen business from savings and customers with no loan. Keeps learning every new tool and keeps his fit-out job until the firm can replace it.
S4.quote: I can't make a man change if he doesn't want to.
S4.fieldNote: The decade lets him build the business without borrowing, so he's calm. His only regret is colleagues like Kasim who won't adapt; he'd offer a job but believes change must be chosen. He doesn't picture himself ever fully sitting still.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because offices would dry up before I'd built anything else, and I'd be starting a firm at sixty with only a few months behind me. What would help is easy finance to lease the new machines for small firms, and lower taxes on small businesses while they get going. Then let people like me get on with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who still needs a builder when nobody needs an office. Everyone thinks about who loses their job. I think about who stops buying what I build.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks about who loses their job. I think about who stops buying what I build.
portrait: Diego is a fifty-eight-year-old lead hand on city office and shop fit-outs who uses an AI assistant every day and fits kitchens for his own customers on Saturdays. He believes in markets, hard work and family, and sees steady change as the moment to start his own small firm with leased robots. AGI in two years makes him anxious not about the robots but about demand, because his trade depends on offices that may empty. He'd pivot to adapting homes for older people and build a firm to hand to his son Marco, taking careful risks but never with the family home. He wants government mostly out of the way, apart from apprenticeships and cheap finance.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because office work would dry up before he'd built anything else, leaving him starting a firm at sixty with only a few months' savings.
whatWouldHelp: Easy finance for small firms to lease the new machines, and lower taxes on small businesses while they get going.
